subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF TRIBUNAL TO AID IN SETTLEMENT OF STRIKES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on an important and urgent matter.
Considering that for several years now, as a result of labour's legitimate claims Canadians have suffered the aftereffects of a number of strikes in the public and quasipublic sectors; that mechanisms did not appear adequate to solve trade disputes in these sectors; that representations made to the government have too often resulted in government intervention through legislation to force workers to return to work, and that such a situation generates conflicts to the detriment of the Canadian public and the economy, conflicts that could be avoided, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser):
That a permanent tribunal of arbitration in conflicts of public interest be established to provide the assistance needed to parties involved to avoid strikes that are far too prejudicial to the Canadian economy. The terms of reference of this tribunal would be to meet the parties, promote better understanding between them, suggest solutions and, if need be, make its recommendations public.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Since the Quebec government has developed special programs, including one entitled "Mission Quebec 1976", in order that the ratio of Quebec athletes taking part in the Olympic Games can reach 30 per cent of the national delegation, and since Canadian delegations for all Olympic sports seem to systematically disregard Quebec athletes, whose ratio would now reach hardly 15 to 20 per cent of the delegation, could the minister tell the House whether he intends to have an inquiry into this so as to ensure a fair proportion of Quebec athletes taking part in the Montreal Olympic Games?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF EQUITABLE PARTICIPATION BY QUEBEC ATHLETES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been very happy to notice, in the last few years, the growing interest shown by the Quebec government in amateur sport and its promotion. Clearly, the Quebec government has allotted considerably
Oral Questions
larger amounts of money to that field in the last few years than in the past.
Still, it is clear that the selection of athletes who will take part in the* Olympic Games is not based upon geographic, linguistic or religious ratios. The choice is made through national competitions sponsored by national sports organizations, and I really believe it would be wrong to intervene politically with a view to having proportionate representation by area.
Now, if there should be cases of discrimination, I should like to be advised of all the details, but every case brought to my attention to date and looked into seriously failed to prove that there had been any discrimination whatsoever.
Should there be such cases, be they British Columbia, Newfoundland or Quebec athletes or athletes from any province, I want to assure the hon. member that we would look into this very carefully, but we will nevertheless continue to rely on national sports federations to select the athletes.

The reason for the warrant was not because we wanted to find out the contents of the letter- obviously we had copies of it-but to get the exact copy that was sent to the Toronto Sun so that we could get evidence as to where it was produced, how it was produced and who might have sent it. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
That this House, believing that the continuing tendency of this administration to reckless and at times contradictory intervention in the economy has created an atmosphere of uncertainty and lack of confidence with the public, and seeing that this uncertainty has resulted in rising unemployment, falling productivity, and unacceptable levels of real growth and inflation, expresses its lack of confidence in the government.
He said: Mr. Speaker, 769,000 persons are unemployed in this country. That is a national disgrace and a tragedy for those involved.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: With the unemployment level at 7.4 per cent nationally, and as high as 14 per cent in the province of Newfoundland, there can be no greater evidence of the failure of this government in its economic policies or lack thereof.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Thousands of students coming into the labour market this summer now face the bleak prospect of little summer employment. This is inexcusable. Worse still, it may have lasting repercussions in that many of these students may not be able to complete their scholastic program without the revenue they had hoped to earn in the coming summer months.
Today, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) simply said, in answer to questions on this important subject, that the government was addressing itself to the problem. That is shameful. What has the government been doing in the past 10 or 11 years that would give the Prime Minister the nerve
Economic Conditions
to stand in this House and say they are still addressing themselves to the problem?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
The present administration leaves the impression that it is not concerned with unemployment because, after all, those who are out of work are cushioned with their unemployment insurance benefits. How shortsighted an attitude, when we bear in mind that some $4 billion is being expended on unemployment insurance benefits, compared to $758 million in the year before 1971 when the Unemployment Insurance Commission program was revised! We are now placing, and continue to place, an intolerable burden on those who are employed in this country, on the businessmen of the nation and on the taxpayers themselves who have to pick up the residual of benefit payments. This is an intolerable burden that need not have occurred had the administration been more prudent in handling our economy. That is the important thing to remember, and that is the thing this administration forgets.
It is not enough to say that those who are out of work are somehow not too badly off as long as their unemployment insurance benefits continue. The fact is that everybody loses when we have needless unemployment and the wealth of the nation falls. The important thing to which this government has not reacted to date is the review of the Economic Council of Canada entitled "People and Jobs". In that review it is pointed out that unemployment insurance revisions have now placed us in the position of being the most generous-if you like, the most liberal- industrialized nation in the world, having regard to our insurance benefit system.
The review points out that the eight-week minimum period after which one is entitled to draw unemployment insurance is by far the lowest minimum period of any nation with which we have to compete internationally. It estimates that .7 of 1 per cent of the unemployed-roughly
70.000	people in this country-are out of work, so far as the records are concerned, because they rely on an overly lax unemployment insurance system. The government knows this. It has hinted it may bring in legislation to tighten up the situation. I call upon the government to produce the legislation that has been talked about to tighten up the laxness in the unemployment insurance system that was so properly outlined in the Economic Council's report to which I referred.
We could perhaps not only save up to $350 million of that $4 billion of unemployment insurance benefits to which I have referred but, more important, it would ensure another
70.000	people who would be working and gainfully employed, which in turn would ensure that even more people would be employed.
That is the type of inconsistency to which we refer in our motion today in which we are asking members of the House to vote non-confidence in this government. Let us take a look at the last two years under this administration. I refer to 1974 and 1975. In those two years, in terms of real growth we have lost $330 for every man, woman and child in this country. That is the cost of the fall of real growth
95568 - 17)4

May 12, 1976
Economic Conditions
during those years. This nation, with our resources, with our trained people and with our agricultural lands, should be able to achieve a minimum of 5 per cent real growth per year. We have not been reaching that level since 1973. We did reach a 5 per cent minimum growth level on average per annum in the previous 20 years, but in 1974 we fell short by 2.2 per cent, and in 1975 we fell short by 4.8 per cent. Maybe that is the reason the former minister of finance was fired. That 7 point drop to which I referred in 1974 and 1975 represents $7.7 billion in our gross national product which has been lost and which I suggest must be regained for the sake of the Canadian people. This shortfall of $7.7 billion, $330 for every man, woman and child in the country, goes hand in hand with today's unemployment.
This is the challenge facing the administration today: Get our people back to work. Get our real growth to a trend level of at least 5 per cent per year. Let us remember that the $330 per annum that is being denied the average Canadian today through the mismanagement of our economy by the administration is almost $1,000 per Canadian family. They should not be called upon to make that sacrifice for the mismanagement of this administration. That is the loss to Canadians as a result of the ineptitude of the administration which I should like to outline in some respects today. In getting our people back to work, we consider the private sector should be the primary supplier of jobs.
We would hope that in the forthcoming budget the administration will orient itself to magnify the influence of the taxpayers' money by providing more jobs in the private sector. For instance, we should allocate research and development funds to the industries that will dominate the future. One example would be solar energy, in respect of which a small investment-small, certainly, in relation to the way this administration likes to spend money-in research and development money can result in a very rapid increase in the number of jobs, literally tens of thousands of jobs for Canadians which could be created in that field alone. Such research and development should be encouraged by private industry in the regions of Canada where our unemployment is the highest.
At the present time, why should private industry in the United States and Canada be opening research and development offices in the Irish Republic, taking advantage of their tax incentives, when such activity could just as easily be taking place in our Atlantic area? Knowing the way this administration acts, I have no doubt that Air Canada is flying such people to create new jobs in Ireland right over our Atlantic provinces. This administration must recognize that it is not further government participation or intervention, nor is it further massive government make-work programs, that are needed. It must recognize that what is needed is restoration of confidence in our future.
It is imperative that the administration should stabilize its position. It should encourage the setting of suitable goals and policies, and then let the private sector get on with the job of reaching the goals to which I have referred. It is the administration's task to set the atmosphere within which the economy can flourish. It is the private sector which should be called upon to produce the results.

In speaking about the incompetence of the government, let me first touch on our debt management. On page 94 of the Economic Review that was recently tabled, the following is pointed out:
Direct and guaranteed government-sector borrowing, which had more than tripled in 1974, increased by a further 35 per cent to $11 billion in 1975.
In short, we have had in the last two years a phenomenal growth in our debt so far as the federal and provincial governments are concerned. I suggest that growth in public debt has placed a needless pressure on the private sector and on the capital markets and has resulted in interest rates going up, to the disadvantage of all Canadians. I suggest, also, that indirectly it has created the unemployment we deplore so much. This load is perhaps more accurately reflected if we look at page 88 of the Economic Review. There, lo and behold, the government boasts about its Canada savings bond campaign. It states:
The 1975 Canada savings bond campaign in the last quarter of 1975 was highly successful. It raised $3,182 million net new cash.
It is further stated:
At the end of 1975 they represented 42 per cent of total government of Canada debt outstanding, compared with 40 per cent in 1974-
That Canada savings bond issue has done two things. It has tended to sop up the mortgage funds in this country which otherwise would go to private institutions for use in housing construction and the refinancing of present homes. The Canada savings bond issue is a contributing factor to the relatively high mortgage rates in this country, almost three percentage points more than we find, for example, in the United States. The second thing that I would point out about the government's handling of Canada savings bonds type of debt financing is that now they have, as is stated in the review, 42 per cent of the debt in this nation on a demand basis. That is not prudent.
Last evening, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), when questioned on this point, agreed that in the current year he hoped that this tendency to such a heavy orientation to Canada savings bonds type of financing would be moderated. I am glad they have come to their senses, but I ask: Why did they not come to their senses in the earlier years when this problem was building up? Again, dealing with this question of credit, I would like to refer to page 99 of the Economic Review which points out that our banks are perhaps in the tightest liquid position they have ever been in their history. The review points out that the preliquid assets ratio showed an even greater relative decline in 1975, falling from 10.1 per cent in January to 8.1 per cent in December. In short, we have basically been running a credit-oriented economy, with the government leading the way in debt expansion, to the disadvantage of all Canadians and indirectly it has created and contributed to the unemployment that we deplore.
Speaking about the handling of the government debt, I think that we, as members of this parliament, would not be responsible if we do not recognize what has happened, for example, to the huge pension funds that are being administered by the government of Canada, and the provincial governments. The fact is that these pension funds have been used, over the past few years, 100 per cent to finance
May 12, 1976

government operations. We now know, through actuarially sound studies, that within three years the outgoings from these pension funds will be greater than the income. The net result will be that unless contributions to the pension funds are increased, there must be some type of a tax subsidy to honour the pensions that will be drawn from these funds in succeeding years. I think it is important, when we are analysing the economic situation in the country, that we not cloud these issues.
Let us look at what the government of Canada has done with respect to the pension fund in relation to our civil service. It is common knowledge that they borrow from the pension fund of civil servants. In private industry it is illegal to do that. No company in Canada is allowed to set up an employee pension fund and then turn around and borrow from the fund in order to operate and, in the case of the federal government, to help cover a deficit that they need not have run up in the first place. This is the type of inconsistency that we feel warrants the members of the House stating they have had enough, that they have lost confidence in this government and that they will support the motion we are suggesting today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Another broad question is the general one of the government's interference with the business community, the over-regulation of business. I may, perhaps, bring this aspect of government activity into focus by referring to a recent article reporting a confrontation between Mrs. Ostry and Mr. Barkway. Mrs. Ostry is quoted by the Canadian Press in an article which reads in part as follows:
Canadian businessmen continue to wrongly regard government competition regulations as illegitimate interference in their affairs, Sylvia Ostry, Deputy Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, said Friday.
"Businessmen in Canada refuse to accept that competition policy is an ally of business... its central role is to strengthen private enterprise.
Then Michael Barkway, in effect, put her in her place. On the same platform he stated:
It seems to me there is great semantic confusion about the word competition. Your department believes in market forces-
He was speaking to Mrs. Ostry.
-until the point where it doesn't like them, and doesn't consider them to be in the public interest.
The article continues:
Mr. Barkway said business could not accept the government's position that firms should not be allowed to extend their market position or power.
"How else can competitive forces operate?" he asked.
He went on to point out the irony of having a government that feels it ought to regulate competition in the private sector while its own bureaucracies find themselves competing for both power and the taxpayers' dollar.
We urge the government to cease the habit of overregulating the private sector and then expecting that sector to produce results, including the jobs that we need in this country. I suggest that the administration hesitates to tell the Canadian public what they foresee in our future. Last evening, the Minister of Finance stated that unemployment would not go below 7 per cent this year. He
Economic Conditions
hoped inflation would go down to 8 per cent. He stated that our real growth would be from 4.5 per cent to 5 per cent. The minister would not even hazard a guess as to what might happen in 1977.
By contrast, the administration in the United States is now required, by law, to bring in a budget, not just for 10 months or 11 months as we will have on May 25 this year: in the U.S. they are required to bring in a budget for the following two years. They also, by habit, give an indication of the future five years as far as the American economy and the budgetary position are concerned. There is absolutely no reason why this administration should hide their activity, as they have been doing, with a shroud of secrecy. They must have their own analysts; this information must be available to them. Surely they are not operating completely in a vacuum. Why will they not reveal to the members of the House and to the public of Canada what they foresee our future will be? In this connection, the Institute of Policy Analysis of the University of Toronto states:
Unemployment this year will be 7.4 per cent by the fourth quarter and 7.7 per cent by the fourth quarter of 1977.
That is most alarming. They anticipate that our real growth over the next three years will not even start to catch up on our seven-point lag to which I referred earlier. They see growth in 1974 and 1975 at only 4.8 per cent and 4.4 per cent, respectively. Let me put it another way. If the institute is correct, we are now, in May of 1976, in the middle of a five-year period in which each year we will have a real growth below our capacity. By 1978, if the trend continues and if the figures that the institute estimates to be realistic are achieved, we will be 10 per cent below capacity, which will represent 300,000 Canadian jobs that will not be available and that would be available if this administration were handling the economy properly-300,-000 Canadians out of work through the shear incompetence of the present administration!
This failure in achieving our desirable goal of a minimum 5 per cent a year will be felt most severely by our younger people who should have every reason to believe that jobs will be available when they require them. With more prudent economic management we could achieve fuller employment and less inflation than is now contemplated by the government.
Let us look at some of the further inconsistent policies this administration has followed in recent years. It is these policies which are creating our problems today. They have put us out of phase with the economy of the United States. Let us think of the repercussions of that. In deciding not to counter inflation in this country until a year and a half after the Americans had moved to counter their inflation, we now find, for example, that our exports have fallen but our imports have remained relatively high. As a consequence, the trade deficit, with which we are all familiar, has heightened. Mr. G. V. Jump, of the Institute of Policy Analysis at the University of Toronto, has said that export growth will be the chief stimulus to increase output and employment over the coming quarters. But what is the position in which the administration has put our exporters? I suggest that they have been saddled with an

May 12, 1976
Economic Conditions
unrealistically high dollar in relation to the American dollar.
The administration has failed to facilitate sales effectively throughout the world, and in fact has jeopardized many of our Canadian industries through poor negotiations in GATT. As the administration makes our exporters less competitive, and even harms our existing industries, it deprives the people of future job opportunities which they would otherwise take. These trade problems resulted in a trade deficit of something like $5 million last year, and a further $5 billion this year. Speaking of last year, the trade deficit was more like $8 billion. This is how the administration had to cover that type of deficit: it first sold almost $3 billion of non-renewable resources which we will never have again. That is how the administration covered $3 billion of the $8 billion deficit it had with the rest of the world.
Second, the administration encouraged the borrowing from foreigners of $4.7 billion, which in turn will aggravate further balance of payments problems because we will have to pay interest of approximately $400 million year by year on that staggering amount. Third, it allowed our foreign exchange reserves to run down by approximately $400 million. That is the present administration in action. How can this House have any confidence in it?
Let us again look at the tourist imbalance. That is perhaps another example of what has happened as a result of our economy being out of phase with the American economy. Last year, our deficit on the tourist account alone was some $700 million. And what do we find? The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, in reference to tourism, proposed to spend $1 million less this year than it did the year before, in spite of the fact that our tourist deficit had jumped $400 million. How inconsistent can you get in governmental action?
Again we have the odd situation that, faced with an imbalance of over $700 million with regard to tourism, we now find, to use the words of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) in the question period today, that for obvious reasons the government is going to see there will be greater scrutiny of those coming into the country. Frankly, the reasons are not obvious to me. It is not obvious to me why there should be greater scrutiny of over 30 million people who come to this country year by year.

It is certainly not obvious to me why there should be that type of discouragement of those who would ordinarily want to come to this country as tourists and who, if they did come, would perhaps lower the deficit to which I have referred. In this time of inconsistency, which I feel is very great, I am a little surprised that even hon. members on the administration side do not realize that it is time they put the nation a little ahead of political expediency and did not support this government any longer.
Let me touch on the question of the government's handling of our money supply. In the Economic Review, at page 91, there is an interesting chart which shows the money supply trend and growth since 1972. I recommend that hon. members take a look at it, because if they want to

see the clearest indication of why we went through, and are in, the inflationary period we are, they do not have to go past that chart. The inflation we had in Canada was substantially political inflation inspired by a federal government which could not control its own spending, and as a result allowed the money supply in this country to grow at too fast a rate.
Last evening the Minister of Finance agreed that the money supply growth in the period from 1970 to 1972 aggravated inflation in this country. I suggest the money supply growth, on a 15 per cent growth line since 1972, as this chart shows, heightened that inflationary pressure to which he referred. That is one reason hon. members of this House should support my motion today.
Speaking about inconsistencies, here we have a government which is deploring rising wage levels in Canada, in that the government says they are getting out of line with the United States. That may be so; but who is really responsible? What else does the administration expect, when it has chosen to give our senior bureaucrats $66,500 per year, compared with the highest paid government worker in Washington who earns $44,000. Our federal minimum wage is $2.90 for those over 18 years of age, compared with the minimum wage in, for example, New York State, which is $2.15. The truth is that it is the lead of this government which has

triggered this situation. How can hon. members have confidence in this government when its past record is full of this type of inconsistent action?
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, what could be more inconsistent than having an administration which fought an election on the single plank of being opposed to wage and price controls, then within a year they flip-flopped over and imposed on the entire nation, not a limited wage and price control program as far as time is concerned, but one that is to run for 39 months and could run even longer. Mr. Speaker, the country has lost confidence in this administration. It is time this House reflected that lack of confidence by voting for our motion today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is almost impossible not to support this motion, in view of the inconsistent behaviour of the government in regard to its policies. I wish it were possible to oppose the motion, after listening to the hon. member who preceded me and the paeans of praise that he put forward for the United States as a model for us to emulate. I should hate to see us do that, as bad as our economic performance is, because I do not think the United States have done much better. If anything, they are starting to move in the direction of more public service employment because they have less room in the private sector to create jobs. There are a number of bills before Congress now calling for the government to provide jobs where the private sector does not provide them. Having got that out of the way, Mr. Speaker, you will understand that my support is for the motion in the broadest sense-for the government's inconsistent policies, rather than for some of the arguments put forward on behalf of the motion.
The government has pursued the kind of policies that would make a great television comedy. You will have seen some of those comedies in the past, where a man goes to turn on his hot-water tap in the bathroom and gets symphonic music, or he turns on a gas range and water spurts in his face. This is the sort of thing that has been happening. Let us look at the government's approach to employment, starting with the budget of June, 1975, when the then minister of finance, Mr. Turner, admitted that the world recession was turning out to be more prolonged than expected and that Canadian unemployment had reached 7.1 per cent. It is now 7.4 per cent. He introduced so-called "direct" employment measures. In December, $91 million was taken out in spending cuts designed to reduce unemployment. Just before coming into the House today I noticed, with some interest and some degree of approval, a column by Don McGillivray in today's Ottawa Citizen in which he referred to that budget. He wrote:
Take last year's budget, introduced at a time when the Canadian economy was in the trough of a recession. Instead of doing anything to stimulate growth and create jobs, it raised taxes, energy costs and unemployment insurance premiums.
In September the Bank of Canada began pushing interest rates up, another proven means of slowing economic growth and thus producing more unemployment. In March of this year the bank gave another push upward on interest rates.
In October, the government introduced its wage and price control package, One of the effects was to restrain incomes and so hold down demand at a time when the economy was running well below its capacity because of sluggish demand.
Economic Conditions
In April, 1976, the Economic Review reported:
-there is no doubt that the strength and timeliness of the income support given to Canadians... between November, 1974, and June, 1975, were among the most important factors (in the milder recession experienced in Canada vis-a-vis the U.S.)
I hope the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) listened to that. The only thing that saved us from a depression like that of the thirties was the fact that the economy had built-in stabilizers such as unemployment insurance and the old age pension. Payments were going out to the economy, and that prevented us from the depth of recession felt by the United States which did not have those built-in protectors.
Given that analysis to the Economic Review, the government then cut the indexing of the family allowance for 1976, a measure that would have helped increase family income and would have supported consumer spending. They did not understand the implications of their own support programs. If they had been serious about combating unemployment, obviously they should have maintained purchasing power in the economy, rather than cut these programs. But they went beyond that: they said to all provincial governments that it was time for them to follow federal government policies; that they should cut their support programs and their expenditures for people on the street and let them collect unemployment insurance. In effect, "Let the unemployment figures go up."
They did that with medicare, saying they could not get provincial co-operation and were going to set the ceilings on their own. The provinces started to get the message, and the province of Ontario, for instance, closed some hospitals and threw nurses and hospital personnel out on the street. Somebody will have to pay for that: it will have to come out of unemployment insurance. Meanwhile, the jobless figures go up. If there is a time to prune hospital expenditures-and nobody argues that some pruning does not have to be done from time to time-it should not be done in the midst of the period of highest unemployment since 1951. That certainly does not show any consistency on the part of the government toward its objective of reducing unemployment.
Until the introduction of the Anti-Inflation Board and the government's so-called wage and price controls, they had taken the position that inflation was essential-a demand-pull kind of situation. They fought an election on that position. When they were not saying that, they were saying inflation was caused by international events over which they had no control. There was some merit to their statements at that time; international oil prices had risen by about 400 per cent and food prices, because of world demand, had risen by 200 per cent and in some cases higher. It was quite obvious that the price of raw materials and many of the production factors that we had taken for granted were increasing enormously.
Suddenly there is a road to Damascus, however, and the government moves from Keynes to Galbraith. The analyses change. Inflation apparently is no longer caused by demand-pull; it is caused by cost-push. The justification for the whole AIB program is to deal with cost-push inflation. They were wrong and contradictory in both cases. Mr. Speaker.

May 12, 1976
Economic Conditions
This government seems to want to take extreme economic views. In the original analysis of inflation being caused entirely by international events, they overlooked many elements of inflation that arose in our country and which we could have dealt with. The same is true now when they say that inflation is essentially a cost-push situation. There are still international factors which make inflation an ongoing problem in this country. They cannot deal with it just through the anti-inflation measures they introduced. It is quite obvious they were looking at the consumer price index, and it is clear that the prices that are declining are those which stimulated the inflation of a year or two ago. The price of food has come down, and that is putting a good face on the consumer price index.
In the ten budgets that the government has presented since 1965, only three have come close to achieving its objective. The 1965 and 1966 budgets were supposed to be mildly restrictive in effect, but turned out to be restrictive. The 1967 and 1968 budgets turned out to be restrictive in effect, which was unfortunate. In those years when unemployment began to climb, we needed expansionary, rather than restrictive, budgets. Only once, when the government had been dead wrong in its original analysis, did the government predict accurately. According to Economic Council of Canada figures-and this is not my observation-only three out of ten budgets came anywhere close to achieving the objectives the government had set.
If we look at the government's present analysis, what does it say? The government position is that to deal with present-day inflation and the problems of Canada which are the result of cost-push factors, we need to implement an incomes policy in this country. It is difficult to support a government which begins by saying that it must do something but does not follow through. We can say, I think, that a policy of selective incomes controls can be useful. But an incomes policy, by its nature, is unfair. Without doubt, the government's present incomes policy is grossly unfair to this country's wage and salary earners, as they directly, more than any other segment of society, are asked to pay the cost. You can tolerate unfairness if the result is worth while. I am sure that workers of this country would agree to limit their incomes if it could be shown that by so doing the economy generally would benefit or the entire population would be treated more fairly.
The government can assure fairness only if it does two things, and judging from the way the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) replied to my question during the question period yesterday, he does not intend to do these things when he brings down the forthcoming budget. First, the government must ensure a fairer distribution of income in Canada. At present, income is distributed unfairly. In the last 20 or 30 years there has been virtually no change in the way our income is distributed. Actually, the people at the lower end of the incomes scale have been hit harder by so-called tax changes than those at the upper end. This must be corrected and the government must bring in measures which will lift some of the burden from the shoulders of the lower and middle income groups, to compensate for the injustices created by the anti-inflation program.

The government must do something else and has no excuse for not doing it. It must move immediately to stimulate the economy and to create full employment. I heard the hon. member for York-Simcoe talking about the lead-swingers who collect unemployment insurance. I do not say that all people receiving unemployment insurance are entitled to it, but I ask the hon. member for York-Simcoe to say how he can sort out the people who are entitled to unemployment insurance from those who are not, from those who do not want to work, when there are no jobs. How can he do it when there is a short-fall of almost 800,000 jobs and only between 40,000 and 60,000 job vacancies?
How do you know if a person wants to work or does not want to work? Also, by what right does anyone accuse labouring people of this country of lead-swinging, of not being willing to take a job, when there are no jobs for them? Jobs must be made available. True, abuses have crept into the unemployment insurance system. If there were no unemployment, it would soon be evident who was not willing to work. A man not willing to take a job should not be entitled to collect unemployment insurance. Nobody would defend him. But considering the enormous amount of unemployment in this country, it is unfair to accuse the working man of not wanting to work. When the hon. member accuses the government of inconsistency, I suggest he ought to look in the mirror.
In my view, and in the view of my colleagues, the government's top priority when bringing down the budget should be the implementation of policies to create full demand in the economy. A tax cut for the lower income levels and a demogrant for those who have no income to report is one of the most effective ways of creating demand and getting people back to work immediately.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Many hon. members agree, I think, that our economy must be stimulated. Hon. friends to my right think that you should not do it by cutting personal income taxes or giving demogrants to the poor, which will enhance purchasing power; they think you should do it by giving benefits to industry. We have travelled that road. No government has been more generous to industry than this one in the last two or three years. But their generosity has been wasted, since unemployment has not been higher for 15 years. Industry does not need to be stimulated to produce. Industry will produce if there are customers willing and able to buy what it produces. There is a great deal of unused industrial capacity in Canada, so there is an obvious case to be made for increasing demand.
At present we are using only 79 per cent of our industrial capacity. Obviously, we do not need more machinery, more industrial stimulation, more depreciation allowances, lower corporate taxes and so on; that is not the way to solve the difficulty. We need more purchasing power in this country, purchasing power we lack.
In the past, the government could argue this way, "We dare not stimulate the economy and create full employment because we have demand-pull inflation and by stimulating the economy we shall greatly increase the rate of inflation; therefore we must trade off a high level of unemployment against lower inflation in order to maintain

price stability." Of course, that policy did not work. We argued against it, and events proved us right. The government has no excuse these days. Inflation, according to the government's own definition, is created by a cost-push situation. The government introduced restrictive wage controls to prevent cost-push inflation taking place. The only justification for those controls, if there is any justification, is that they can now be used to stimulate the economy. The government cannot make the hoary excuse that we dare not create full employment because of the effect on prices. But that, apparently, is one of the great inconsistencies to which the government still clings.
My time has almost ended. I wish I had more time to go through the long catalogue of the government's failures. In the past, the government's analysis of the economy has all too often been wrong. Furthermore, analysis has not been translated into policy. All too often the government has predicted wrongly what would happen in the economy. No government can plan perfectly. One cannot expect any government to plan perfectly and implement the right policies all the time. But we insist on there being some logic in the way the government behaves. We say to the government that on the basis of its own analysis of the economy, logic dictates that the budget which is to be brought in later this month should be a full-employment budget, a budget which will enhance the purchasing power of those most in need, people in the lower income groups, in order to get the economy going again.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion retains all its value in the present context of the Canadian economy. I congratulate the official opposition for introducing a motion which is quite relevant and which fits very well the existing conditions in Canada. I quote the motion:
That this House, believing that the continuing tendency of the administration to reckless and at times contradictory intervention in the economy has created an atmosphere of uncertainty and lack of confidence with the public, and seeing that this uncertainty has resulted in rising unemployment, falling productivity, and unacceptable levels of real growth and inflation, expresses its lack of confidence in the government.
Mr. Speaker, this motion tells the truth. On the whole, economists admit that the present economic conditions in Canada are really appalling and the Government does not know where to turn to find solutions.
In fact, according to the latest figures disclosed yesterday, the number of unemployed in Canada is increasing, whereas the governments are contemplating higher taxes and proposing budgets which will require costly loans to repay past debts or merely the interests accrued from those debts.
That is the situation we are witnessing, Mr. Speaker, for even though the goverment suggests it is fighting against inflation we do have rampant inflation, and the Canadian worker, the working classes, the low wage earners are faced with a quite inadmissible situation in a rich country like Canada.
Yesterday, in the paper Le Soleil, we could read this leading paragraph:
Economic Conditions
Ottawa to borrow more this year. Assessing at between $5 and $5.5 billion the federal government treasury needs for the 1976-77 financial year, Greenshields Inc. stated yesterday that this year Ottawa will have to borrow 37 to 54 per cent more than last year.
That is nice increase. And even if the gouvernment says that the inflation rate did not rise as much this year as last year, we will see in a few months to what extent inflation rates will have gone up at the expense of the people of Canada in general.
Mr. Speaker, only a few months ago we heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say that we would live in a new society, that in that new society we would see things unknown to us, new things we never dreamed of.
We already have entered this new society where private entreprise, private property is threatened from all sides, where free enterprise is also threatened from all sides by government controls. The only place where employment is up today is the public service, the administration of the federal government. There the number of new jobs is frightening, while private companies or free entreprise must slow down production because, as the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) said a moment ago, consumers do not order goods because they do not have the money to do so. Prices increase continuously; we have just been informed of an increase in the price of gas, of oil for July 1; it is reported that gas may even cost $1.25 a gallon.
Mr. Speaker, the government is the first to ignore the legislation they produced or the Anti-Inflation Board they built from scratch a few months ago. Yesterday, we were advised of a terrible jump in the price of coffee because there was a drought in Brazil; it may even cost $5 a pound. If there is a drought in Brazil, there is perhaps no drought in Jamaica or in other coffee producing countries. The price of sugar also threatens to go up. Is there a lack of sugar canes? Of course not. There are also reports about higher prices for wood products. This morning, I ordered four by four cedar posts and they cost 67c. a linear foot which means that ten feet cost $6.70, and this is fairly small.
Mr. Speaker, the same thing happens everywhere. What does the Incomes and Prices Board or the Anti-Inflation Board have to do with that? It is all very well to appoint civil servants and hire people and new bureaucrats to look over or study the results obtained by the old bureaucrats, or other bureaucrats hired before them, but what results do we get? It is the same thing in every sphere.
When one sector is poorly managed, right away Ottawa is asked to help. For instance, the Olympic Games in Montreal. Ottawa was practically forced to set up a permanent national lottery to make up the deficit that should not exist at this point because, several years ago, I had the visit in my office of the Mayor of Montreal and His Excellency Mr. Rousseau who came to give me the plans for the Olympic Games and prove, figures in hand, that the Olympic Games would finance themselves through the Olympic lottery. We all accepted that but today we find that it is not so, far from it.
I said a year and a half or two years ago that the Olympic Games deficit would reach $1 billion. I was told I was crazy, that I could not count.

May 12, 1976
Economic Conditions
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Quebec budget proved clearly that the deficit is now $1 billion, and the games have yet to be held. When they take place, we will reach the billion and a half, because they are a bottomless pit. That is inflation! The Olympic Games will cost at least four or five times the amount we were told they would. That is a problem. As for James Bay, we are embarrassed to talk about that one. I said that this development would reach $20 billion. But people said no way, Caouette can't add.
Mr. Speaker, by now we have reached $15 billion in expenditures at James Bay, while that project was to cost $6 billion at best. Outlays are expected to total $15 billion and the end is nowhere near. When the work is finished over there, we will have a debt of about $20 to $25 billion. Then, suppose for instance that the James Bay project will cost $20 or $25 billion, say with a 10 per cent interest rate over a 25-year period. Do they know that in 25 years we will have paid $50 billion in interest alone, and we will still owe $25 billion. This will mean a total of $75 billion. Will our great-grand-children have finished to pay by the end of their lives? No.
Billion of dollars are spent here and there without considering a terrible system forcing Quebec, municipalities, school boards and the federal government to borrow fabulous sums at astronomically high interest rates. The Montreal Olympic Games will probably cost $2 billion at 10 per cent interest over a 20-year period. We shall still be paying $4l/i or 5 billion in interests only. And we will still be owing all the money that was put into the Olympic venture.
Mr. Speaker, it is about time the federal government should find other alternatives. We have been suggesting a variety of them in this House for 40 years; some thirty years ago, in 1946, I suggested to the House those very same solutions. In those days, our opponents, the Liberals and Progressive Conservatives, 'were laughing at me. Given the present system, if we replace the Liberals with the Progressive Conservatives, what would be the result? Would the interest rate be reduced? No. Both are supported by the same financial "gimmick". The federal government will have to borrow, this year, 37 to 54 p. cent more funds than last year.
But why borrow when the federal government has the authority to take action? Parliament can decide, because of its supremacy, to call upon the Bank of Canada and cash in on the physical facilities we have in Canada to develop our natural resources and create a financial and economic system which would guarantee each human being a decent life. That would put an end to labor conflicts such as the ones we now have. Day in and day out, all we hear about is a strike here and a strike there, federal strikes, provincial strikes, strikes everywhere. Nobody is satisfied. And the federal government says: we are going to satisfy everybody; we are going to organize bingos, lotteries, provincial lotteries, federal and municipal lotteries; church bingos. Then, we become a nation of "racketeers" as they say in English. This is opium to the poor: You see a fellow without a penny in his pocket or he may have a dirty old five dollar bill left and his wife is off to a bingo where she expects to win $6.50. Then, as usual she does not win anything; she has no money left to buy bread or butter for

her children but she does find an old five dollar bill in her purse to go and play bingo.
Mr. Speaker, we are living in bingo territory. See what goes on in Montreal. Mr. Bourrassa himself will be allowed to play bingo in the province of Quebec. In Montreal, it is the same thing: Loto-Canada is not too readily accepted across Canada, by the other provinces. They say: "Wait a minute! You were supposed to finance this thing! Now, see to it! Then, we are going to ask the people in Vancouver-I understand that anyone is free to try his chance at the lottery, to buy a ticket or not, but we provoke people with our publicity on television, in newspapers: "the next mil-lionnaire". There are people who are too poor to have their three meals a day, but they find the money needed to buy a ticket that will turn them into millionnaires. Everybody is so happy the day of the draw because millions of people think they will be the new millionnaires. Six or seven million people will have paid in to make one, two or three millionnaires.
Mr. Speaker, when we have come to the point of adopting such a system, do you not think that it is rather frightening? What can happen? Anything. If we look at what is now happening in the world, in Beirut, in the Far-East, in the Middle East, in Italy, in Spain, in Portugal, we realize that things are getting out of hand. People are no longer responsible. They do not care to be. Are our union leaders responsible people? They ask for salary increases which bring about price increases. Our workers gained nothing. They went on strike. If they did not have their present jobs, the strikers would beg for them. Once they get them, they strike again.
This goes to show how bright they are! This is the labour situation in the province of Quebec. They want jobs, and as soon as they get them, they let themselves lured into striking action. It is said to be bright, but I call it criminal. In Canada, in Montreal, or anywhere else, the strikes now prevailing are the direct consequence of the economic system but those people are not even interested in changing the economic system.
When election time comes, they say: Liberals are better than Progressive-Conservatives, then they vote for the Liberals. After, they get mad and go on strike. At the next election, they may vote Progressive-Conservative.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Salts-man) said earlier that under the Progressive Conservative government, we had a million unemployed in 1961, and that this happened in spite of the fact that we had the strongest government Canada has known since Confederation. This is why the Diefenbaker government was defeated, because of the unemployment rate in 1961. And the very same people today are saying that they would do better than this government. Come on! The same causes have the same effects. We must change the causes and not the parties. What do we get when parties change? If we are all caught by the neck and choking to death, nothing is changed.
Mr. Speaker, we must change the economic system, and this is why we have been making the following suggestion to the government for such a long time. Instead of borrowing from the United States or other foreign countries, and asking their permission to benefit from the development of our own natural resources, why do we not use the services

of the Bank of Canada, which is authorized to create money legally and intelligently according to our needs? Then we could say that our natural resources belong to us and not to the Americans. These resources belong to Canadians!
Mr. Speaker, people do not understand this. They think that Social Credit is something odd and they refer to the strange kind of money that Social Creditors advocate. What kind of stupid money do we now have? We do not have any, and we are always begging from the Americans the right to develop our own natural resources. It is quite a farce to see Mr. Bourassa paying his weekly visit to New York to borrow money to finance the James Bay project! Do the Americans lend money to Mr. Bourassa because he is Mr. Bourassa? The provincial government, and the federal government, say: The province's credit is good. Canada's credit is good. Canada's credit is so good that we may well sink the country all the deeper in debt. Its credit is good.
When Mr. Bourassa calls on the Americans, they do not say to him: "Mr. Bourassa, your smile is so inviting, your hair is so nicely combed, you were so well made up before you went on television." No. The Americans ask: "What is your collateral for borrowing $150 million? What about the natural resources of James Bay?" The Americans are no fools. They look at those ressources and say: "This is good, this is profitable, this will become extremely good. Therefore, we shall lend $150 million, not on the basis-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext: A good collateral!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Yes.
They do not lend money on their own property, they lend $150 million against a note signed by the provincial government which puts up all the natural resources of James Bay as collateral. Why should we go to the United States to do so, instead of going to the manager or the governor of the Bank of Canada and say: Listen, take the same resources, James Bay, the same thing; come up with a figure according to our needs to develop James Bay. Would that not be legal? Instead of paying an interest of 10, 11 or 12 per cent, we might have this credit from the Bank of Canada at cost, which would mean approximately 1 per cent, Vz of 1 per cent, % of 1 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, why does the government not act in this direction? When the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance are telling me that our credit is good, the Liberals clap their hands. They do not understand a thing about it but they still clap their hands. Let us keep on voting for the Liberals and continue selling-not selling, but giving away our natural resources to the Americans. And then we are amazed and shocked to see that the number of unemployed is increasing in this country.
That is another matter. Reference was made earlier to the unemployed. I look forward to the establishment in Canada of work insurance to develop our potential. We have roads, hospitals, public buildings to build. We have houses to build, homes rather than hostels for the aged, rehabilitation centres for our young delinquents, centres where they could be educated, taught a sense of duty and responsibility. When asked for government help, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde)
Economic Conditions
answers: There is no money. So things worsen, the young go to prison. This is costing enormous sums of money to the Canadian taxpayers. The government has no other solution but to encourage that kind of system, to maintain and finance it.
Mr. Speaker, it is time we stopped to think. Inflation comes from somewhere. It is not caused by too many products, but by not having the purchasing power to acquire them. Private enterprise is in jeopardy. The private sector, private business, free enterprise, everything is being sent down the drain. The young are not interested any more in using their abilities, because they are tired of working for the government's sake and paying taxes. Mr. Speaker, down with the tax system, down with the debt financing system created by Grit and Tory governments in Canada since Confederation. Let us have freedom, let the day come when credit and resources are controlled by us in Canada, not by the Americans.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me, I would like at the outset to read the motion again to be sure that my eyes have not deceived me. I quote:
That this House, believing that the continuing tendency of this administration to reckless and at times contradictory intervention in the economy has created an atmosphere of uncertainty ...
-and I underline "uncertainty", with your permission-
... and lack of confidence with the public, and seeing that this uncertainty has resulted in rising unemployment, falling productivity, and unacceptable levels of real growth and inflation, expresses its lack of confidence in the government.
After careful consideration, Mr. Speaker, I take the liberty of reminding you that on March 24, the hon. member for York Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) moved a motion almost identical to this one. But at that time, he spoke of rashness and uncertainty.
I would also like to emphasize the fact that he has not invented anything, since, as late as last night, the same hon. member asked questions to the minister when the finance committee was considering the economic review of Canada and he then had the opportunity to question the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). He used about the same terms he has been using ever since he first came to this House. Therefore, I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the uncertainty, the rashness and everything else he is talking about did not stem from the positive action of this government but rather from what the hon. member has attempted to spread in the world of business and labour and at the other levels of government.
I remember quite well that for many months the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), kept urging either the Prime Minister or the then Minister of Finance to act. Now that steps have been taken, they ask: Why did you do that? You have done the wrong thing, you have created a climate of uncertainty. Perhaps those people should decide exactly what they want.
Having faced the situation, I feel the government has taken clear positions. Members are certainly aware of the Anti-Inflation Act brought in this House and discussed at length. I think there has been concerns expressed by several members. Some were asking that certain points be clarified and the legislation has even been amended. It is not
13454

Economic Conditions
easy for a government to respond to a situation, particularly in the business field, and I readily admit it. But having examined the complexity of the Canadian economy, the government has realized that there were some sharings which were not fair.
I think it was the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) who said a moment ago that the distribution of wealth between the members of society was not fair. This was a valid point, I suggest, and it is precisely because the government took measures in various fields that there is now a more equitable distribution of wealth in Canadian society. Perfection is not of this world, but we can certainly aim at it and I try to improve that situation through the different projects put forward by the government.
As regards business, many labour organizations have said that business was not affected, that it did not know what was going on and that the manufacturing industry could do as they liked. Therefore, I think I must point out that the facts are quite to the contrary. When the AntiInflation Act was first implemented, it was perhaps true to say that the regulations affected some workers more than some industries.
It was necessary to require a report to test such a system. The reports having been submitted, we certainly noted the reaction of the business community which promised to go along, to submit reports, since the government had established guidelines not for salaries but also for the industries. The names of some industries not affected by the legislation were even suggested to the government. They now come under the act.
Members opposite were so kind as to fail to mention the improved economic conditions in Canada. In the report of the Economic Council-and I shall wait until later to quote from it-we see that compared to the situation in other countries, namely the United States and our main competitors: Japan and Germany, the economic climate in Canada is different and better than in most of our closest competitors. I must readily admit, Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, that there is surely room for improvement. It is not easy. It must at least be recognized that in 1974-75 we faced a world-wide crisis which proved far more serious in the countries I have mentioned than it was in Canada. The government, having initiated those measures, must assume the responsibility for them, and I believe that every member should at least try to give the policies now under discussion and the legislation which was passed a chance to work out.
Last night, as I said earlier in the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, the opposition certainly did ask some questions but without breaking new ground, without suggesting anything new since the introduction of a motion by the same member last March. What they did was only to interpret some statistics, and I should like to stress at this point that it is not the statistics that are false, because they appear in the report, they are available, they were made public and everybody studied them, but it is their interpretation that is false.
The motion itself deals with productivity. I think that chart No. 9 in the Economic Review deals with productivi-

ty. There was certainly an improvement, as shown in the chart. Several conclusions can be drawn, but it should at least be admitted that there is a great deal of improvement, and members opposite should admit it. I referred to the world situation; it must be kept in mind that the Canadian economy, Mr. Speaker, is certainly affected by the world situation.
Our exports, 50 per cent of our manufactured goods, end up on the international market. If the situation I mentioned earlier resulted in 1974-1975 in a strong tightening in most of our trading partners, its impact was certainly felt in Canada.
Since then, the situation has changed. Now, they will not admit it, they talk about tragedies and what not. But let me very briefly point out a sudden turn which happened in the U.S. car industry. Particularly since 1965-66, Canada and the United States have entered into an auto pact which was worth while and needs to be readjusted-our officials are busy at it at present-but it should be said also that in the last few months, car sales in the United States have increased by more than 50 per cent.
The same thing happened in Canada. This has certainly resulted in a fairly large increase in car sales not only in the United States, but in Canada as well, since our industry supplies many parts to various factories and various companies which trade in Canada and in the States under this agreement.
Reference was made earlier to imports and I wish to deal with this subject as well. It is normal and healthy that people affected by imports should react. But if imports were to increase, Mr. Speaker, our domestic economy had to be such as to allow the import of some goods. In certain cases, they were not manufactured goods, but in others, the need was real.
A number of semi-manufactured goods which are not available in Canada have to be imported. For most countries I mentioned earlier, we had no choice and had to restrict our imports and in several cases cut them altogether. In so doing, we had to consider the well-being of their people has not reached the same standard as in Canada. Within our domestic economy, the inflationary trend I indicated continued, during the world crisis and is still being felt today.
Canada, and especially the government, is not satisfied with the results, though they are better than elsewhere; by all means, it wants further improvements. If we refer to the reports of the Economic Council of Canada, to those of Statistics Canada, in spite of the bitter criticism we heard from the other side of the House this afternoon, we see that the curve indicates a decrease in food prices despite the increase in wages. I will talk about that later if I have enough time.
I will deal briefly with employment because you know that the time allocated is rather limited. There are now more people working than never before in Canada. Statistics, which I could give you, although I believe that is not the purpose of the debate, show that millions of people changed jobs. Almost six million individuals changed jobs, in some cases volontarily, but others changed because industries have evolved and had to adapt to new products.

I think that by taking the necessary decisions, the government helped many of these people improve their situation. If you refer to the same report of the Economic Review, you will see that with the hourly increases, wages went up rather substantially-alarmingly in some cases. The increase was much higher. I do not say that they did not deserved it, but it was much higher than that of our closest competitor where go about 70 per cent of our exports. This is only one factor which prompted the government to clamp controls on wages and prices.
Productivity was also mentioned. I dealt with that a while ago. I even told you in which diagram you could find it. This productivity is obvious. Now, it may be considered that statistics are not always accurate. There were also- and I think this is one of the factors that must be mentioned-negotiations at that time. Either because of unions which were not asking everywhere for wages unrelated to productivity, or of employers or manufacturers who were charging prices that bore no relation whatsoever to the real market value of some items, the government had to step in. That is what it did, because all the economic factors were considered and then a decision was made. As soon as the decision was made, the Official Opposition started to clamour. This afternoon, I took the liberty of reading it out so that everybody will realize that the words used do not quite reflect the facts.
Having said that, I think that the decision made was a fair one. Companies realized-they were affected as well- conscientious employers did the same, followed by unions which, in most cases, I think, are adequately meeting their members' demands, that they had to face the actual situation, the economic position. They realized they had to negotiate not only an agreement from the viewpoint of the strongest economic element, but a real agreement designed to enchance the well-being of all Canadians, and in my opinion, the success and strength of Canada lie in three-party negotiations.
As regards inflation, I will only mention a few facts. If you look at statistics, you will find a real decrease in the inflation rate. Such facts are glossed over perhaps. Then, our friends opposite mentioned a few, but as the rate decreased, people outside the fields I referred to earlier, who do not take part in negotiations, namely retired people, low-wage earners who were among those most strongly urging the government to act, and that is one of the factors we considered when making our decision.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to read an excerpt from the Economic Review, on page 5 which deals with the fiscal and monetary policy. It is a paragraph that was overlooked by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and which surely describes in a very clever and accurate manner the real facts, and I quote:
Fisbal and monetary policies were adjusted in 1975 to the changing cyclical and inflationary situation, The November 18, 1974 federal budget provided substantial fiscal stimulus to the economy, mainly to take effect in 1975.
Provincial budgets ...
This is a point which was missed earlier when we were talking about governments. I carry on with the quotation:
Economic Conditions
Provincial budgets in early 1975 added significantly to this expansionary thrust. Following the unsuccessful efforts in early 1975 to obtain a consensus of price and income restraints to cope with inflation, the June 23 federal budget began the process of government expenditure restraint intended by itself, and as an example, to offer Canadian spenders an opportunity to contribute to slowing down inflation. On a national accounts basis, expenditures on goods and services and capital formation by all levels of government increased 5.2 per cent in real terms in 1975, compared with 7.9 per cent in 1974: government expenditures increased at a slower annual rate of 3.1 per cent during the second half of 1975, compared with 5.8 per cent during the first half.
I could carry on as there are in this page many indications yet of the thrust given not only by the central government but by various levels of government with the results that are mentioned here. Now, I am concerned about some points in the remarks made by various members of the Opposition and I would like to come back to them. Mention was made earlier of the various government programmes and one in particular. Then it was quickly mentioned that the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) in particular in the figures he quoted, had omitted to say that the central government had made provision for a redemption, commitment and a redistribution to maintain the price of oil and then the price of heating oil at a much lower level than the world price. But that was not mentioned.
However, this favourable situation is appreciated by the consumer. But some of our colleagues do forget what has happened. The honorable member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) spoke about family allowances.
It is true that they were not escalated but he did not mention that in his expenditures the government had previously tripled the amount of family allowances. Rather than being selective, I think I must recognize this quality in the hon. member for York-Simcoe but I did not know the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge had it. Instead of being too narrow-minded, we should bring true facts to this House and discuss them further, and I would be the first to listen but in those areas, figures should be chosen carefully. We can quote figures all day long but without ever coming to the facts. This is what I wanted to emphasize, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Yes, even if I think it is not the expression used in the motion, "shameful" expresses the point very well. If we go back to 1961, it is quite a long time ago, but at that time there was a Conservative administration-I did not say so, but the hon. member for Waterloo-Cam-bridge (Mr. Saltsman) did-and a million persons were unemployed.
I would invite the hon. member to see exactly what those people had at their disposal. When you are unemployed, most of the time it is not because you asked for it. This was mentioned earlier. People wake up one day without work and without revenue. I have often seen that either employers in some cases or unions in other cases are not quite willing to meet the demands of the unemployed.
But the unemployment insurance program was established by this government. It was said earlier it is abused. One needs only to add the figures. But that money was redirected into the economy, which forced large budgets upon the federal government. If there are abuses, as is often indicated, instead of sounding off loud statements, some effort should be attempted to find a way to direct the money within the budget to those who really need it because their plant was shut down, and maybe because their union would not negotiate because its emphasis is on some segments only in society, or because the employer himself wanted skilled labour. The federal government, through the manpower department or the unemployment insurance program, saw to it that employees or employers be confronted with reality. How are those moneys spent? This is what was to be determined when reference was made to huge sums of money. It is a fact. Maybe we should think it was for the well-being of society, and not because the government wanted to intervene in some area just for the fun of dealing with astronomical budgets.
It was indicated earlier that the Unemployment Insurance Act should be amended in depth. It should be remembered that there was an outcry by the majority of the people, especially in this House, when we discussed the legislation and amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. We heard other suggestions then. It may be allright to level criticism on a motion like this one, but when comes the time to vote on some legislation it is a different story altogether. Reality and speeches are two different things.
Reference was made earlier-and the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) also mentioned several funds-to pension funds. It is true that the government and governments, Mr. Speaker, use funds to finance certain projects both within the federal government and provincial governments, and that money is redistributed. The hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette), who has left, suggested using the Bank of Canada. That is a means of financing government projects, not only at the federal level but also at the provincial level. Only one province escapes that rule, the province of Quebec. The hon. member, I think, is smart enough to understand that if at some point your commitments exceed your revenues, a different program must be considered-an increase, differ-

ent deductions. One must also think that those pensions give people a safeguard that did not exist until the government decided to provide it. Some of our colleagues made speeches-you certainly heard them-and said they wanted 40 per cent of the salary earned. The government plan gives about 25 per cent. I ask the hon. member to tell me if it is too much to ensure an employee who, in most cases, has no other income, 25 per cent of his salary. If that is the point he wants to make in this House, I think that is a shameful response. It is certainly not the attitude of this government.
Reference was made to creating jobs through the private sector. I agree with that idea-it was mainly the hon. member for Simcoe who raised the subject-and he has no difficulty convincing me. There are two other points that I should like to make. The first concerns job shortages forecast for 1980. I believe that the facts are quite different and that in certain areas, there will be a shortage of manpower rather than hundreds of thousands of unemployed. Maybe we should consider the fact that manpower departments exist to recycle people who did not have the opportunity to go to school so as to be able to face the realities of the labour market.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to close by saying this: We are faced with a concrete situation, the Canadian economy is improving, government programs have shown this, as have figures quoted in the Economic Review, in the report of the Bank of Canada, members of the European Council and other visitors have come here to congratulate the government and the Canadian people for having shown some discipline, and everything that has been done is now having these results, and I am certain that with the cooperation of all members of the House, we shall continue to control inflation and ensure that Canadians will find employment in their chosen fields.
