subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO SOLVE ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the previous speaker, my hon. friend from Montreal-Bourassa (Mr. Trudel), who made a good speech on behalf of the Minister of Finance.
It was a difficult speech to make. The minister's absence clearly shows the lack of interest of the government in our economic problems, but I want to ensure the House that the problems mentioned in the resolution of my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), are quite serious. It is difficult to understand the attitude of the Liberal government. Now, Mr. Speaker, I prefer to continue in my mother tongue.

In the motion before us today attention is drawn to the words "reckless ... intervention in the economy." I suppose we could consider it another example of reckless lack of intervention when the minister ignores the debate which is going on here today.
There seems to be little disagreement that inflation is a serious problem in Canada. However, I am not sure that the government realizes it, that there is only one cause and that the federal government is the only body which can cause and create inflation. All inflation comes from expanding the money supply. Credit is not inflationary, because credit is created by someone producing wealth and being willing to defer the consumption of that wealth. For example, when an individual borrows money, he can borrow it because someone else has produced wealth and is willing to forgo the spending of it at that particular moment.
The same is true when business borrows, when civic governments borrow or when provincial governments borrow. In every case the borrowing is created by someone having produced wealth, saved that money and not spend it. Therefore, there can be no inflationary pressure. One is simply trading one type of spending for another type of spending. But when the federal government borrows, it simply creates more money by paper entries in the accounts, and that is where the inflation comes from. Inflation is a little bit like pregnancy, because although there are many facets to the problem of inflation, just as there are to the problem of pregnancy, in each case there is only one cause. On that there is not much disagreement in Canada.
I refer the House to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Hamilton last December. This was before his famous speech. He said:
Yes, we could bring down inflation to proper levels In 18 months. But If we did It would mean tightening the screws so much and so fast, that we'd then be causing a slowdown in the economy and massive unemployment even more serious than we have now. So, it's possible to bring inflation down very quickly by tightening up very drastically the money supply, by having a very conservative fiscal policy and so on, joined to the guidelines.
In other words, the Prime Minister was saying that he knows what the cause is, but he was also saying at the same time that he was unwilling to accept the consequences of taking action to solve a problem of which he knows the cause. It might cause us to wonder why it took until now to recognize the cause of inflation. We have been operating under this administration for 13 years, eight of those under the present Prime Minister. The Prime Minis-

May 12, 1976
Economic Conditions
ter was supported in his views by Professor Lawrence B. Smith of the University of Toronto, who made a statement which the Globe and Mail considered important enough to carry in an editorial. Referring to inflation, Professor Smith said:
There is really only one explanation for our present inflation ... namely that there has been too fast an increase in the rate of growth of the money supply.
If we all agree on the causes of inflation, then we should be able to agree on the solutions. I should like to refer to some of the other results of our anti-inflation policy in this country. First of all, many demands are caused by inflation, although people usually state it the other way around. The wage earner is forced to seek higher wage settlements so that he can keep up with inflation; merchants are forced to seek higher prices in order to protect themselves. The Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants together urged the government to make tax changes which would involve more than just indexing of exemptions. That would be some help, of course, but they feel that further steps are necessary in order to make permanent solutions available to taxpayers.
One thing they suggest, for example, is expansion of the limit of contributions made to registered retirement savings plans. Limits for those contributions were set in 1971 and have not been changed. They suggest that we need relief from taxation of illusory gains on property. If those things were done, the revenues of the government would fall. But this government wants to spend more money, so it is not hard to understand why it is reluctant to do these things. In Canada, savers pay taxes on their investment income, which is at times less than the rate of inflation. A prime example is Canada savings bonds. The government borrows money from taxpayers, taxes the income which is usually interest at about the same rate as inflation, and they pay capital back later in deflated dollars.
I have referred to reckless, and at times contradictory interventions. I should like to give a few examples of interventions which are hurting the people of this country. There was an article in the Financial Post of May 1 concerning the annual meeting of Bell Canada. It says it is a pity that the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board was not at the meeting. If he had been, the article says-[DOT]
He would have heard that big audience-1,225 of them, all ordinary, mostly elderly folk-stirred to applause by only one statement.
The article says that Bell's chairman described the AntiInflation Board's refusal to approve Bell's eitht-cent quarterly dividend increase as a "mistake". This decision directly affected 210,000 shareholders, most of them, as I have said, small investors and pensioners who rely on the dividends. It is interesting to note that Bell Canada is 98 per cent Canadian-owned. Most of them, as I have said, are little people and about 140,000 own fewer than 100 shares, for an investment of approximately $4,500. The company wanted to increase the dividend by 9.3 per cent, which is less than the rate of inflation last year. They were denied the increase. The minister has said that the Anti-Inflation Board would allow increases in dividends when justified, and one of those times would be if a company needed to raise additional capital for expansion. That was the ground

on which Bell Canada made its application to raise additional capital, but even so it was refused.
Another article in the same issue of the Financial Post referred to the new rules of the CRTC concerning FM programming and the restriction of the number of commercial minutes to be sold by those stations. I do not want to get into a debate on that rule at this time becasue it does not apply here. It is interesting, however, that the CBC itself was exempt from the new rule, while independent operators lost advertising revenue at a time when costs of new programming were increasing. The anti-inflation guidelines prevent stations from raising their rates to compensate for loss of revenue.
Mr. Speaker, I have already referred to government intervention. The remarks of the Deputy Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, made last week to the Financial Executives' Institute in Ottawa, is a case in point. Dr. Ostry said:
Businessmen in Canada refuse to accept that competition policy is an ally of business ... its central role is to strengthen private enterprise.
Mrs. Ostry said that the pending revision of the Combines Investigation Act is not intended to be a detailed intervention in the economy but, rather, is to assist consumers and business in their respective activities in the marketplace and is "an alternative to more direct government intervention".
Mr. Speaker, the government holds that more intervention is an alternative, but they persist in taking the view that it is possible to help both sides at once. Anyone who has been involved in an adversary relationship knows that cannot be done. I think the Prime Minister indicated that he did not entirely disagree when he said in his famous December speech:
It's a massive intervention into the decision-making power of the economic groups and it's telling Canadians we haven't been able to make it work, the free market system.
That is the famous "free market" statement which I think gave him a lot of problems. I do not see how businessmen or individuals in Canada can think otherwise, given the government's intervention in the marketing of foodstuffs, for example. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) tells us that the purpose of marketing boards and controls is to avoid "highs" and "lows". We know that, because now all we have is "highs" and no low prices at all.
The millions of taxpayers' dollars that the government invests in unnecessary Crown corporations is a type of intervention. Take Canadian National Railways being in the hotel business, for example. That may have been necessary 40 years ago, but today we have plenty of good hoteliers who can make money and we do not need the government's intervention.
Radio is another example. These days there is no need for taxpayer^ to subsidize radio to the tune of $200 million a year. Many radio operators in Canada are prepared to build and provide the service. We have only to look at the telephone industry to realize that a simple licensing system would enable the government to ensure the service is provided without being in the business itself. There is also Petro-Canada which competes with the oil companies.
There are many examples. Another example is public works which come under a government department and
May 12, 1976

not a Crown corporation. The department claims to be able to provide office space to the government at low cost through facilities it has which are not available to the public sector. The work of the Auditor General made it quite evident, I think, that the success of the Department of Public Works is questionable, at best, and that there should be an alternative method of providing space. I believe that private enterprise could do it quite well without tying up millions of taxpayers' dollars. I do not know how Canadians can react any differently in face of the government's attitude to situations such as this.
That brings me to the second part of the motion, which refers to uncertainty and lack of confidence with the public, which has led to "rising unemployment, falling productivity and unacceptable levels of real growth and inflation ... " The uncertainty must apply particularly to young males under 25 years, among whom unemployment is far greater than among those in the over 25-year old category. Of course, there are reasons for that. But do we hear suggested that the government's follies are at the root of these reasons? For example, this government offers the most generous unemployment insurance benefits in the world. There is absolutely no encouragement to work more than eight weeks. People are encouraged not to work. Therefore, a whole generation is growing up with no incentive to work.
In Vancouver, where we have the Habitat forum-it is to be an adjunct of the Habitat conference-there is an able man by the name of A1 Clapp who has men nearing the age of 30 working for him, for low wages admittedly; but these are men who in most cases have never before had a job. I have a son at the University of British Columbia and hear all these stories about jobs university students cannot get. My son has a job. When he told his employer that he wanted to quit his job in August so that he could take a few weeks off before going back to university, the employer begged him to stay because he could not fill the job. We have heard of tens of thousands of jobs being available. I can only point my finger at this government and say it must change the circumstances which cause these jobs to remain unfilled.
The Economic Council of Canada has recommended that government jobs should be created and that benefits be cut off if they are not accepted. The Economic Council discovered that in 40 per cent of cases, unemployed people called on for a job interview did not show up. They were not interested. If one is offered a suitable job and does not accept it, one should not be entitled to benefits. In a case like that, benefits should be cut off. These kinds of abuses have been referred to previously. In 1975, unemployment rates, on average, were 15 per cent for males under 25 years and 10 per cent for females in the same age bracket. These young people represent one half of our unemployment statistics but only one quarter of the labour force.
It has been observed that in Canada the working poor make up a large percentage of all the poor. The poor work, and the young lie around and work only long enough to collect their benefits. That is the fault of the attitude this administration had instilled. I remember the postal strike of 1974, or was it 1975? I am not sure which year it was: we have a strike almost every year. I know that thousands of
Economic Conditions
unemployment insurance cheques were left unclaimed in Toronto because their intended recipients were not able to travel downtown to pick them up.
The Economic Council of Canada study entitled "People and Jobs" says on page 5;
-the minimum annual rate of unemployment rose from 3.6 per cent in the 1960s to over 5 per cent in the 1970s and, in periods of slack demand such as experienced recently, the unemployment rate exceeded 7 per cent-
But, during the early 1970s, job vacancies climbed significantly without much moderation in the unemployment rate.
On page 6, the study says:
Despite the recent slackening in output, Canada's rate of real growth averaged 5 per cent annually over the last ten years. However, most of this was due to employment growth rather than productivity increases.
If we cannot get people to work, there will not be any productivity increases. It continues:
Since 1963 Canada's growth in output per man-hour has been consistently lower than that of all other OECD countries, except the United States.
I now turn to page 21, which deals with attitudes. The study found that Canadians are strongly motivated to work and said:
The vast majority of Canadians would prefer suitable work to unemployment insurance, but about one out of three would accept unemployment insurance rather than work at the minimum wage-

speechtext:
There is evidence showing that foreign investors wish to invest in this country. FIRA, the foreign investment agency, has been screening applications for some time and their number has remained constant. This means that foreigners look at Canada as a place in which they want to invest. I ask the hon. member, who is not in his seat, if he interprets that as uncertainty and lack of confidence. Every year, hundreds of thousands of would-be immigrants from all over the world try to come to Canada. Is this evidence of lack of confidence and uncertainty on the part of people throughout the world who look upon Canada as the place to which they want to go? Obviously, the answer is no. These three examples show how superficial is the motion, and the hurry with which the hon. member for York-Simcoe probably drafted it. If there is any lack of confidence, I suggest it is between the two ears of the hon. member himself.
Let us consider another part of the hon. member's motion. The hon. member spent some time talking about unemployment figures. I ask if he has ever taken time to look at employment figures. For instance, has he considered the increase in employment in Canada? For instance, in the period 1971-72, 236,000 new jobs were created in this country; in 1972-73 we had 394,000 new jobs; in 1973-74, 393,000 new jobs; and in the time from 1974 to the third quarter of 1975, we saw well over half a million, precisely 552,000 new jobs created in this country. Was the hon. member looking at that kind of evidence when he drafted his motion?
For instance, did he look at comparable figures applying to OECD countries? We learn, that our great neighbour to the south, whose population is ten times greater than ours, in the period 1974-75 created only 214,000 new jobs, or less than half the number of new jobs created in Canada. In the eyes of the hon. member for York-Simcoe, is that performance poor? Did he, for instance, look at the number of new jobs created in Australia, where the number of people employed in 1974-75 actually went down? In Canada, the number went by over half a million. In France in the same year, zero new jobs were created because employment went down. The same applies to Germany and Switzerland. In the eyes of the OECD, a neutral agency that looks at things above and beyond the political scene, Canada's performance was excellent, as reported by these employment figures.
What did the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) look at in order to arrive at his motion that speaks of uncertainty and lack of confidence? He speaks of rising unemployment. Did he also look at the phenomenal figures for rising employment? The same applies to levels of real growth which have been described by the OECD as among the best in the western world. They have been better than that of the United States. Over the years it has been among the best in industrialized countries. Where did the hon. member for York-Simcoe get his notion, information, facts or statistics on which to base his motion? It is difficult to say.
The motion also speaks of reckless intervention. Does the hon. member for York-Simcoe think that the AntiInflation Board is a reckless intervention in the economy? If so, why? Perhaps that is the reason he and his party

opposed the amendments to the Anti-Inflation Board Act to provide an appeal procedure for labour; they were passed last week. If it was a reckless intervention, why did the hon. member for Lanark, on third reading, support the Liberals and vote with the government? He must have reached the conclusion that it was a measure worth supporting and not a reckless intervention on the part of the government.
What about tax reform? Does the hon. member for York-Simcoe consider that to be a form of reckless intervention? What about the solid system of unemployment insurance in this country which protects those in the poorer areas in Canada, areas where unemployment is not available on a year-round basis? Does he consider that a reckless intervention? Is that the platform of his party? Is that what he is going to tell the people of New Brunswick, Saskatchewan and Ontario at the time of the next election?
Does the hon. member for York-Simcoe think that direct job creation on the part of the federal government is reckless itervention? Does he think that subsidies to the aircraft industry to maintain its Canadian nature and provide employment for 8,000 to 10,000 aircraft workers is a reckless intervention? If so, why does he not say it? Does the hon. member believe that legislation with regard to foreign publications, like that which removed tax concessions for Time magazine and others, was a reckless intervention? That measure benefited Canadian publications as well as radio and television stations.
Is the hon. member for York-Simcoe against this kind of intervention on the part of Ottawa? If so, what intervention does he think the federal government, on behalf of the Canadian community, should introduce to stimulate the economy, protect the weaker elements in society and maintain Canada's position in the world? If you travel throughout the world, you are told by people of other countries that Canada is one of the finest countries in the world because it has been able to retain a good standard of living and a fine economy.

speechtext:
That is one of the most popular cliches, that you cannot have it both ways, but it happens many times. At any rate, when 5.45 comes it will be the motion for which we are voting, not the speech of the mover. The hon. member for York-Simcoe said something in his speech that I did not like. This is the reason I asked for about four or five minutes. He got on to the subject of pensions, and even though he was speaking to a motion that talks about uncertainty and lack of confidence, he said the sort of things that might increase those very conditions.
What I took exception to in particular was his complaint that the federal government is too free with pensions, that it escalates the pensions of public servants, RCMP and armed forces personnel, and so on. As the hon. member for York-Simcoe would have it, things are going to get out of whack. The fact is that the fund for the payment of escalation additions to pensions is still in the black. It could get a little below the line if it were not already part of the law that, starting January 1, 1977, the contributions to that fund will be 1 per cent rather than one-half of 1 per cent. Therefore, I see no danger of any trouble in that regard.
The hon. member was simply mouthing the kinds of complaints that we see in the Globe and Mail, a newspaper which frequently says nice things about me on its editorial page. However, in this area I beg to disagree. The complaint is that public servants, and others who come under federal jurisdiction get an escalation in their pensions due to the rise in the cost of living, which is something which others do not get and, therefore, is unfair.
By sheer coincidence, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) yesterday placed on Hansard an answer to a series of questions of mine bearing the number 5,026. These were questions having to do with private pension plans. Although I have known from previous research that the situation was pretty bad, I was really shocked to discover that so far as the government is able to capture-that is the government's word-the statistics, 82 per cent of the individuals in Canada today who are working and are in pension plans are in plans that provide for no escalation after retirement. The other 18 per cent are provided with a certain amount of escalation, in some cases equal to the rise in the cost of living, and in other cases less than that figure.
I should like to say to my hon. friends who write for the editorial pages of the Globe and Mail, to those who deal with pension matters in the financial publications of this country, and to those who represent big business when they attend the Canadian pension conference, that what is wrong with the pension situation is not the fact that public servants and a few others have their pensions escalated so as to keep up with the cost of living; what is wrong is that all of the rest do not get the same escalation.
I insist that the time has come when it should be the rule that a pension is not a pension unless after retirement arrangements are made for the pension to be indexed or escalated, so when people retire they can at least keep up with the rising cost of living. I think they should be able to do better; I think they should be able to keep up with the
Economic Conditions
rising standard of living. Indeed, I should also like to see the industrial composite applied to the escalation of pensions rather than just the rise in the cost of living.
I promised my friend for Prince George-Peace River that I would not trespass on his time, but there was this one point I wanted to make. Although I am going to vote with my colleagues for the motion of the hon. member for York-Simcoe, I did not like the attack that he made today on public pensions. I think they provide the lead to this country and that it is time pensions in the private field matched those in the government field. Or if that is not possible, it is time that consideration was given to enlarging the Canada Pension Plan so that eventually all our people will be covered under government pensions that are secure, rather than under private plans which in so many cases are insecure and which, to the extent of 82 per cent, according to the figures placed on Hansard yesterday at page 13395, do not have any escalation.
That is my point, Mr. Speaker. It is not a mistake that some get escalation; the mistake is that so many do not get it. I hope that we can soon correct this unfair situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I address myself to the motion that is before the House, if Your Honour would allow me I should like to say this in response to what was said by my colleague from Winnipeg who spoke ahead of me. If we ever did realize his dream, which incidentally I share, and all Canadians in our society are assured of a comfortable life after making their contribution to this country and they retire from the active labour force, then we must ensure we also have a healthy business climate. In the context of modern-day pension guarantees, we must also ensure that this country has a healthy corporate business climate.
What my colleagues to my left often overlook is that all pension plans invest in corporations and business, including the pension plans that the great unions of this country

Economic Conditions
maintain on behalf of their membership. In order to guarantee a comfortable income through pensions we must continue to create the kind of climate in which corporations and business can flourish within a society such as ours.
It is incredible to witness a government that is so far removed from the reality of today, Mr. Speaker-a government that has not recognized just what is going on in the economic world outside. The government has completely overlooked the fact that our major trading partners, including those who share the North American continent with us, have brought their inflation under control. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) overlooks the fact that the international con game of inflation is over. The government fails to realize that we are only cheating ourselves at this time when we think our trading partners will continue to accept our watered-down dollars, because they are losing their value. They are being passed on to those on fixed incomes and who receive sustenance payments from the federal government, such as senior citizens' allowances, unemployment insurance, family allowance and that sort of thing. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the international con game is over. We no longer have access to the global community. The European Economic Community has the problem under control, and so has the United States. We are fooling no one but ourselves.
One of my concerns at the present time is the lumber and wood fibre industry in this country. In terms of the deficits with other countries that it has been chalking up in recent years, there was a deficit last year of $5 billion, and it will be even worse next year. Most of the trade in wood fibre products is with the United States, and they are gaining a $5 billion trade advantage every year with this country. The United States enjoys a positive trade balance, particularly with iron curtain countries, as a result of its trade in agricultural products. Our lumber and wood fibre industry will be facing very stiff competition in the United States in very short order because that country will have to correct its trade imbalance with Russia by exporting lumber and pulp products to that country.
It is no secret that our productivity has declined and that the price of our lumber products has increased to the point where it is very difficult today even to compete with producers in the United States, never mind those who import from across the ocean. It is hard to believe lumber grows on trees any more, in view of the price of it these days. This is why we are all so concerned, particularly when you consider that the lumber and wood fibre industry is second only to our great agricultural industry. I fear for my country when the time comes that we will have to face the inevitable and use our wood products within the country only because we have priced ourselves out of international markets.
The problem of inflation, in my humble opinion, is not the number one problem, even though it is the cause of even greater problems which we are facing today. I refer particularly to the industrial warfare being waged in our country. One must remember that this country, with its potential, its great natural resources and the great heritage we enjoy, has achieved the dubious distinction of having the worst record in industrial relations. This is due to this

government's incompetence and to the people who elected this government instead instead of a group of people who offered a solution to the problems of inflation and the situation in which we find ourselves today.
This government waited too long to bring in prices and incomes controls, and when it did bring them in it was the wrong program entirely. The government has lost the trust and confidence, not only of the individuals in our country but, more particularly, of those groups which have the power to exert undue pressure on our economic system. I am talking particularly about the unions which have opted out or dropped this government as a lost cause and are setting out on their own causes, protecting their own interests.
Industrial warfare is being waged in this country to an extent that frightens me. It frightens me because I think of the record of those major industries which are performing essential public services. I refer to the railway which operates throughout the province of British Columbia, the work force of which is represented by eight different unions, each one capable of shutting down the operations of the railway. I ponder the question of what happens to the other seven unions which are not on strike. The members are, of course, on unemployment insurance while the strike is on.
It is for this reason I suggest the system has reached the point where it is consuming itself. This is no longer spiralling inflation but a crumbling of the foundation of the system which built this country and at one time made it great. We are in a situation today over which we have no control. The only solution to the problems which are even greater than inflation now, namely, those problems associated with industrial warfare and strikes which are destroying the welfare of this state, is a change of government.
This government has lost the confidence of every Canadian. It has removed itself from the will of the people and from the realities of modern times, to the extent that it should no longer have the right to bring any programs before us which are not in tune with the needs of our times. This government has removed itself from the principles of international markets and has totally ignored the programs which initiated the turn-around the people in the United States are experiencing. You do not have to go very far to see this: just walk across the border and order a meal.
